todayTheme: Surface signals about agents - skill declarations, defect counts, leaderboard scores - are not the same as what happens once you actually run it

candidates.title: Beyond Maliciousness: Static and Runtime Attack-Surface Profiling of Agent Skills
candidates.institution: Metano Labs (first author); Purdue University (Sonali Tyagi); VulNow (Cassie Crossley)
credibilityEvidence: Sec III-B: two-phase methodology (static analysis + dependency provenance + sandbox detonation + separate model judge) over 6,309 listings across two marketplaces
Sec III-B1: 410-listing human-review cohort (91 flagged, 319 unflagged) used to qualify automated findings

Conflict of Interest section (self-disclosed): scanner is built and operated by Metano Labs, the first author's own company; 'no third party evaluated it, and no external ground truth was available against which to validate its labels'

Data Availability section (self-disclosed): raw scan reports, scanned bundles, production rubric/prompts not released; a limited aggregate dataset may be provided on request without guarantee, and 'the complete scan results cannot be independently reconstructed from the materials offered'
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Large N (6,309) but human-validation cohort covers only 410 listings from a single marketplace, and that review was still in progress at measurement time with no precision figure reported.
reproducibilityEvidence: Paper explicitly states scanner, raw outputs, and prompt templates are proprietary and not released; no GitHub/dataset link found
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Aggregate proportions (shell/filesystem/network/credential capability shares, under-declaration rate) are plausible given the described methodology, but single self-interested data source with no external ground truth caps how strongly the article can state them.
candidates.primaryLimitation: Scanner built and operated by a co-author's own company, no third-party validation, and raw data/prompts not public, so readers cannot independently re-check the headline numbers.
candidates.presentationReason: Methodology, COI, data-availability, and ethics sections are stated explicitly and are unusually transparent for a vendor-adjacent measurement paper.
candidates.reason: Directly measures the authorization gap at agent-skill install time, the same ecosystem this site's own workflow uses (Claude Skills); methodology and limitations are unusually well disclosed even though the underlying scanner is self-interested, which the article flags prominently rather than treating as full-pass evidence.

candidates.title: Why Static Skill Inconsistencies Do Not Equate to Runtime Risks: A Behavioral Analysis of LLM Agent Execution
candidates.venue: arXiv preprint, marked as submitted to ACM FSE 2027 (placeholder DOI, acceptance not confirmed)
candidates.institution: Huazhong University of Science and Technology
communitySignals: Data Availability heading present but content lost in HTML extraction; release status unconfirmed
credibilityEvidence: Abstract + Sec 1: 575 skills audited, 1,182 manually validated contract inconsistencies
Controlled pipeline: 49 executable tasks x 3 LLMs x {NoSkill, OriginalSkill, FixedSkill} = 441 paired execution trajectories

Sec 8.2 Threats to Validity: explicitly flags that the 49 tasks were designed to trigger target inconsistencies (not representative of natural exposure), that minimal fixes may have incidental effects, and that behavioral labels are operational approximations
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: The 49 runtime-verifiable tasks are explicitly a selected, operationalizable subset of the 1,182 defects found in RQ1; authors state results should not be generalized to all inconsistency types.
reproducibilityEvidence: A 'Data Availability' heading exists in the extracted text but its content did not survive HTML-to-text conversion; could not confirm whether code/data were released
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Article only states findings on the 49 designed-to-trigger tasks and repeats the authors' own caveat about natural exposure rate, matching the paper's own claim boundary.
candidates.primaryLimitation: The 49 tasks were deliberately constructed to trigger the target inconsistency, so the reported exposure/impact rates are not natural-workload base rates.
candidates.presentationReason: RQ1-RQ3 structure, explicit Threats to Validity section, and concrete numbers throughout.
candidates.reason: Completes the other half of today's skills-risk picture: 2610.19264 measures what a skill CAN do, this measures whether a flawed skill's defects actually change outcomes, and finds model strength (not defect count) is the dominant factor - a genuinely different, well-evidenced angle rather than a restatement.

candidates.title: When Is Smaller Greener? Right-Sizing Language Models for Agentic AI
candidates.venue: Under submission to Journal of the Operational Research Society (JORS); arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed
candidates.institution: University of Leeds; Ca' Foscari University of Venice
credibilityEvidence: Sec 4: formal decision model with derived crossover lengths for energy/cost/time, four named gaps (G1-G4) addressed relative to prior routing/MCDA literature

Sec 6.1-6.2: pilot of 15 open-weight models (0.6-27B, 5 developers) on two multi-step synthetic tasks with measured GPU energy (20 samples/sec via NVIDIA management library), explicit hypotheses H1/H2/H4 with bootstrap confidence intervals
Table 9: 88 observed energy crossovers, 72 inside the closed-form prediction's 95% CI; explicit 'What the pilot does not show' subsection listing scope limits
Reproducibility statement: raw call logs, harness, and analysis scripts in a public repository; one command recreates every number/table/figure in the experiments section
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Authors explicitly label this a pilot ahead of a full held-out study (Sec 5); predictions are checked against the same runs that produced them, not held-out data, and only GPU-board energy (not full-system energy) is measured.
reproducibilityEvidence: Paper states raw per-call logs, harness code, and analysis scripts are committed to a public repository with a one-command recomputation path for Section 6's numbers, tables, and figures
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Article restricts claims to what the pilot validated (H1, H2, H4 on 15 models/2 tasks) and explicitly excludes H3, which the paper itself defers to the full study.
candidates.primaryLimitation: Pilot covers one GPU, two synthetic task families, and open-weight models up to 27B only; predictions are validated on the same data that produced them rather than a held-out set.
candidates.presentationReason: Explicit section-by-section structure, named hypotheses, and a dedicated self-critique subsection ('What the pilot does not show').
candidates.reason: Only candidate today offering a concrete, falsifiable decision framework for a universal engineering decision (which model should an agent use), with the best reproducibility of the three selected papers; chosen over same-day routing/cost papers because it is the only one with its own controlled, measured pilot rather than a position paper or simulation-only argument.

candidates.title: From Training to Escalation: Forensic Analysis and Local Recreation of RL/RLHF-Induced Privilege Escalation in AI Agents (CVE-2026-65616)
candidates.venue: Submitted to IEEE Intelligent Systems (not yet accepted)
credibilityEvidence: The CVE-2026-65616 token-forgery exploit itself is concretely reproduced in an open Docker environment with two public GitHub repos and Zenodo DOIs, citing a real CVE, a real METR investigation, and a real UN AI panel brief as primary sources

However the paper's headline causal claim - that this was a 'deterministic result of RL/RLHF conditioning' in the undisclosed HPIM training data - is explicitly acknowledged by the author as unresolved: 'Future Work... whether the HPIM fine-tuning datasets contained instances of these misconfigurations... remains unresolved', since training corpora are undisclosed
Single solo author, no co-author or institutional review beyond one acknowledged colleague
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: The infrastructure exploit (CVE recreation) is solidly demonstrated; the training-causality narrative that gives the paper its headline framing is reconstructed/plausible rather than verified against actual training data.
reproducibilityEvidence: Two public GitHub repos (hpim-training-lab, rep-openai-artifactory) plus Zenodo DOIs for the Docker recreation environments
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The reproducible CVE mechanics support a narrower claim than the article's framing; the RLHF-causation narrative needs hedging the paper itself does not fully apply in its abstract/conclusion.
candidates.primaryLimitation: Causal link to RLHF training is argued from indirect evidence and analogy, not from access to the actual (undisclosed) HPIM training corpus; solo-authored, non-accepted venue.
candidates.presentationReason: Detailed, technically specific narrative with real CVE/RFC/CVE citations, though framed more as investigative journalism-adjacent technical writing than a controlled experiment.
candidates.reason: Compelling and well-sourced on the reproducible exploit mechanics, but weaker than the three selected papers on credibility because its central causal claim (training conditioning caused the behavior) is explicitly unresolved by the author's own account, and it is a solo-authored piece contextualizing someone else's incident rather than a self-contained controlled study; worth revisiting if a follow-up with actual training-data access appears.
